source.title: Michael Faraday, His Life and Work
source.attribution: Silvanus P. Thompson, Michael Faraday, His Life and Work, Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: Read what passes through your hands, not just handle it
cards.body:
Faraday had almost no schooling. At fourteen he was apprenticed to a London bookbinder, and for seven years books passed through his hands all day. Most binders saw only paper to stitch. Faraday read them, and an encyclopedia article on electricity, sent in for binding, first turned his mind to science.

A friend later said he was the best bookworm for eating his way to the inside. The lesson travels well. Your job probably puts useful material in front of you every day: reports, manuals, the expertise of colleagues. You can treat it as stuff to process, or as a free education waiting to be opened.
cards.quote: I said he was the best bookworm for eating his way to the inside; for hundreds had worked at books only as so much printed paper. Faraday saw a mine of knowledge, and resolved to explore it.
cards.locator: Chapter I. Early Life, Training, and Travel ¶7
cards.apply_it: Pick one document, tool or process you handle at work without understanding it. Spend fifteen minutes this week learning how it actually works.

quiz.question: What first turned Faraday's attention to science?
options: An article on electricity in a book he was binding
quiz.explanation: As an apprentice bookbinder, he read an encyclopedia article on electricity that came to him for binding.

cards.title: Test what you read with small, cheap experiments
cards.body:
As an apprentice Faraday delighted in Mrs Marcet's Conversations on Chemistry and the electrical articles in the Encyclopaedia Britannica. He didn't stop at reading. He tried the experiments himself, limited to what a few pence a week could buy, and built his own electrical machine, first from a glass bottle and later with a proper cylinder.

That habit of checking ideas with his own hands became the core of his whole career. You don't need a laboratory or a big budget to learn this way. A small, cheap trial of what a book claims teaches more than a second reading, because you see where the idea works and where it doesn't.
cards.quote: I made such simple experiments in chemistry as could be defrayed in their expense by a few pence per week, and also constructed an electrical machine, first with a glass phial, and afterwards with a real cylinder
cards.locator: Chapter I. Early Life, Training, and Travel ¶7
cards.apply_it: Take one claim from something you are reading and try it out this week in the cheapest, smallest way you can.

quiz.question: How did the young Faraday fund his first chemistry experiments?
options: A scholarship from the Royal Society
With a few pence a week of his own
quiz.explanation: He kept his experiments to what a few pence per week could pay for, and built his own apparatus.

cards.title: Write ideas down the moment they come, wherever you are
cards.body:
In his very first letter to his friend Benjamin Abbott, the young Faraday complained that thoughts springing up in his mind were lost for good because he hadn't noted them at the time. He never forgot the lesson. For the rest of his life he kept a card in his waistcoat pocket and would stop to jot down a note in the street, at the theatre or in the lab.

Ideas arrive when they like, not when you are sitting at a desk. A capture habit, whether a pocket notebook or a notes app, means the good thought on the bus is still there when you can use it.
cards.quote: In his later years he always carried in his waistcoat pocket a card on which to jot down notes and memoranda. He would stop to set down his notes in the street, in the theatre, or in the laboratory.
cards.locator: Chapter I. Early Life, Training, and Travel ¶9
cards.apply_it: Choose one place to catch stray ideas, such as a pocket notebook or a single notes file, and use it every time a thought strikes for the next week.

quiz.question: What did Faraday carry in his waistcoat pocket?
options: A card for jotting down notes
quiz.explanation: He carried a card for notes and would stop anywhere to write a thought down before it was lost.

cards.title: A stranger's small kindness can change a whole life
cards.body:
Faraday's rise depended on people who noticed him. His master, the bookseller Riebau, encouraged his studies. A French artist lodging above the shop lent him books and taught him to draw. His elder brother paid for his first science lectures. Then a customer, Mr Dance, impressed by the apprentice's industry, gave him tickets to hear Sir Humphry Davy lecture at the Royal Institution.

That one gift opened the door to everything that followed. It is worth remembering from both sides. If you are starting out, show your effort, because people do notice. If you are established, a ticket, a book or an introduction may cost you little and mean everything to someone else.
cards.quote: Another frequenter of Riebau’s shop was a Mr. Dance, whose interest in the industry and intelligence of the apprentice led him to an act which changed the whole destiny of his life.
cards.locator: Chapter I. Early Life, Training, and Travel ¶10
cards.apply_it: Think of someone younger or newer than you who is clearly trying hard. Offer them one concrete thing this month: a book, an introduction or a seat at an event.

quiz.question: What did Mr Dance do for the young Faraday?
options: Gave him a job at the Royal Society
Took him to hear Humphry Davy lecture
quiz.explanation: Dance, a customer at the shop, enabled him to hear four of Davy's lectures at the Royal Institution.

cards.title: When you ask for a chance, send proof of your effort
cards.body:
Faraday longed to leave trade for science. He first wrote to Sir Joseph Banks, President of the Royal Society, and got the porter's reply: no answer. Undeterred, he wrote to Humphry Davy, and this time he enclosed the notes he had taken of Davy's lectures, carefully written out and bound in a volume.

Davy replied that the notes showed great zeal, memory and attention. Soon after, he hired Faraday as his laboratory assistant. A request alone is easy to ignore. A request with real work attached shows what you can do. One unanswered letter is not the end of the road either.
cards.quote: induced me at last to take the bold and simple step of writing to Sir H. Davy, expressing my wishes, and a hope that, if an opportunity came in his way, he would favour my views; at the same time, I sent the notes I had taken of his lectures.
cards.locator: Chapter I. Early Life, Training, and Travel ¶21
cards.apply_it: Next time you ask someone for an opportunity, attach one piece of work that shows your effort, such as notes, a sample or a small project.

quiz.question: What did Faraday send Davy along with his letter?
options: A letter of recommendation from Banks
His own notes of Davy's lectures
A bound copy of a chemistry book
quiz.explanation: He sent the notes he had taken of Davy's lectures, which Davy said showed great zeal, memory and attention.

cards.title: Form a small group that corrects each other honestly
cards.body:
Soon after joining the Royal Institution, Faraday and his friend Edward Magrath started what they called the mutual-improvement plan. About half a dozen young men met in Faraday's attic rooms or at Magrath's warehouse to read aloud together and correct one another's pronunciation and use of language.

The criticism was blunt, and Faraday judged the results most valuable. The group ran for several years. You can do the same with a few friends or colleagues working on the same skill, whether writing, speaking or coding. Agree up front that plain, open feedback is the point, and meet regularly enough for it to compound.
cards.quote: who met of an evening to read together, and to criticise, correct, and improve each other’s pronunciation and construction of language. The discipline was very sturdy, the remarks very plain and open, and the results most valuable.
cards.locator: Chapter I. Early Life, Training, and Travel ¶43
cards.apply_it: Invite two or three people learning the same skill as you to meet monthly and give each other frank feedback on one piece of work.

quiz.question: What did Faraday's mutual-improvement group practise?
options: Correcting each other's pronunciation and language
quiz.explanation: They read together and criticised and corrected each other's pronunciation and construction of language, with very plain remarks.

cards.title: Study others at work and judge what succeeds and fails
cards.body:
A few months into his job as a lab assistant, Faraday wrote four long letters to Abbott about lectures and lecturers. He had watched Tatum, Davy, Brande and others closely: their rooms, their tables and diagrams, their delivery, their habits, and the effect each had on the audience.

He didn't expect to lecture himself, yet he reasoned that observing others was the best way to learn, and that you must dare to judge in order to judge well. Years later he became the finest science lecturer in London. When you want a skill, watch people who have it and note precisely what works and what falls flat.
cards.quote: how learn better than by the observation of others? If we never judge at all, we shall never judge right.
cards.locator: Chapter I. Early Life, Training, and Travel ¶50
cards.apply_it: Next time you watch a talk, meeting or performance, write down two things that worked and one that didn't, and why.

quiz.question: How did Faraday first learn about good lecturing?
options: By closely observing other lecturers and writing down his judgements
quiz.explanation: He studied the habits, faults and effects of the lecturers he assisted and set out his conclusions in letters to Abbott.

cards.title: Seeing more of the world shows you how much you don't know
cards.body:
At twenty-two Faraday had never been more than twelve miles from London. Then Davy took him on an eighteen-month tour of France, Italy and Switzerland, where he met Ampère, Volta and other leading scientists. The trip served as his university.

It did not make him proud. Writing home, he said he had learned just enough to see his own ignorance, and felt ashamed of his defects. He took this as a spur, not a blow, and wanted to use every chance to improve. New places, jobs and people can give you that same honest picture of yourself. The useful response is to start filling the gaps.
cards.quote: I have learned just enough to perceive my ignorance, and, ashamed of my defects in everything, I wish to seize the opportunity of remedying them.
cards.locator: Chapter I. Early Life, Training, and Travel ¶75
cards.apply_it: After your next new experience, write down one thing it showed you that you don't know yet, and one step to start learning it.

quiz.question: How did Faraday respond to discovering his ignorance on his travels?
options: He decided to return home at once
He resolved to use the opportunity to remedy his defects
quiz.explanation: He said he had learned just enough to see his ignorance and wanted to seize the chance to remedy it.

cards.title: Hard stretches are often the only road to something better
cards.body:
During the European tour, Faraday was unhappy. Davy's valet had refused to travel, so Faraday found himself doing a servant's duties, and Lady Davy treated him with disdain. Writing to his friend Abbott, he reflected on what such troubles had taught him.

Looking back, he said, things that first seemed misfortunes usually proved to be benefits. He compared them to storms that bring lasting good, and to rough, hilly roads that are uncomfortable but lead somewhere worth reaching. He even felt that hardship kept his mind vigorous in a way easy times never would. When you are on a stony stretch, ask where the road might be taking you.
cards.quote: sometimes they appeared to me like roads--stony, uneven, hilly, and uncomfortable, it is true--but the only roads to a good beyond them
cards.locator: Chapter I. Early Life, Training, and Travel ¶73
cards.apply_it: Recall one past setback that later turned out to help you. Write a line about how, and keep it for the next rough patch.

quiz.question: What did Faraday compare his misfortunes to?
options: Stony, uncomfortable roads leading to good beyond them
quiz.explanation: He likened them to uneven, hilly roads that are unpleasant but the only way to a good beyond them.

cards.title: Comparison makes your life look worse and others' look better
cards.body:
When Abbott, unsettled in his job, talked of leaving to travel, Faraday urged him not to change his situation in haste. A hasty change, he thought, would only make things worse.

He also gave a sharp piece of insight. When you compare your situation with those around you, yours appears sadder and theirs brighter than either really is. The comparison itself distorts the picture. Today that happens every time we scroll through other people's highlights. Before making a big change, check whether your discontent comes from your actual life or from a flattering view of someone else's.
cards.quote: You will naturally compare your situation with others you see around you, and by this comparison your own will appear more sad, whilst the others seem brighter than in truth they are
cards.locator: Chapter I. Early Life, Training, and Travel ¶76
cards.apply_it: Next time you envy someone's situation, list three hidden costs it probably carries and three good things about your own.

quiz.question: What did Faraday warn Abbott about comparison?
options: It is the best way to choose a career
It makes our own situation look sadder and others' brighter than they are
quiz.explanation: He said comparison makes our own lot seem sadder and others' seem brighter than in truth they are.

cards.title: Loyalty to a mentor never means hiding the truth
cards.body:
Faraday owed Davy his career and stayed loyal to him all his life. He had helped Davy develop the miners' safety lamp, a great practical advance. But the lamp was not safe in every condition, and Davy would never admit it.

When a Parliamentary Committee asked Faraday directly whether the lamp could become unsafe, he said yes. It angered his master, but he would not bend the facts. Later, beside an exhibited lamp bearing a glowing inscription, he pencilled: 'The opinion of the inventor.' Gratitude and honesty can live together. You can respect someone deeply and still refuse to cover for them.
cards.quote: Not even his devotion to his master would induce him to hide the truth. He was true to himself in making the acknowledgment, though it angered his master.
cards.locator: Chapter II. Life at the Royal Institution ¶17
cards.apply_it: Is there a fact you have avoided stating because it would upset someone you respect? Decide how you could say it honestly and kindly.

quiz.question: What did Faraday admit before a Parliamentary Committee?
options: That he invented the safety lamp
That the safety lamp could become unsafe in some conditions
That Davy had stolen his work
That he had no scientific training
quiz.explanation: He admitted the lamp could be unsafe under certain conditions, even though it angered Davy.

cards.title: A flawed role model can teach you what to avoid
cards.body:
Davy was brilliant but had almost no sense of order or method, and little self-control. Faraday kept Davy's experiments running, preserved every note he made, and copied his scrawled research into neat, clear handwriting.

Faraday once told a close friend that one of his advantages was having before him a model of what to avoid. He absorbed Davy's genius while quietly choosing the opposite habits, becoming known for scrupulous order in his own work. You can learn from people's weaknesses as well as their strengths, without bitterness and without ceasing to admire what is good in them.
cards.quote: Faraday has been known to remark to an intimate friend that amongst his advantages he had had before him a model to teach him what he should avoid.
cards.locator: Chapter II. Life at the Royal Institution ¶17
cards.apply_it: Think of a boss or mentor you admire. Name one strength to copy and one habit of theirs you have decided not to repeat.

quiz.question: What did Faraday say was one of his advantages in working for Davy?
options: Having a model of what he should avoid
quiz.explanation: Davy lacked order and self-control, and Faraday said having such a model taught him what to avoid.

cards.title: Give self-study fixed evenings each week
cards.body:
As a young assistant, Faraday had no evening duties, and he planned his week with care. Monday and Thursday evenings went to self-improvement, following a regular plan. Wednesdays went to the City Philosophical Society, where he learned and later lectured. Saturdays he spent with his mother, leaving Tuesdays and Fridays for his own business and friends.

The plan protected study without crowding out family or friendship. A fixed slot works better than waiting for free time, because free time rarely arrives on its own. Two set evenings a week, kept steadily over years, add up to a real education.
cards.quote: Monday and Thursday evenings he spent in self-improvement according to a regular plan.
cards.locator: Chapter II. Life at the Royal Institution ¶13
cards.apply_it: Pick two evenings this week for learning and put them in your calendar as fixed appointments, alongside time for family and friends.

quiz.question: How did the young Faraday organise his evenings?
options: He worked in the laboratory every evening
Set evenings for self-improvement, his society, his mother and his friends
quiz.explanation: Mondays and Thursdays were for self-improvement, Wednesdays for the society, Saturdays for his mother, the rest for friends and business.

cards.title: Pay for expert coaching on the skill that matters most
cards.body:
Faraday earned very little, yet in 1818 he paid half a guinea a lesson to the elocutionist B. H. Smart to improve his speaking. He filled 133 pages with notes on the lessons. Later, when he began lecturing in the theatre, he asked Smart to sit in and criticise his delivery, and his friend Magrath came to lectures to note down every fault of pronunciation or delivery.

Natural talent was not enough for him. He sought out expert eyes and kept asking for them even after he was successful. If a skill is central to your work, investing in a coach or a trusted critic is often the fastest way to improve.
cards.quote: In 1818 he attended a course of lessons on oratory by the elocutionist Mr. B. H. Smart, paying out of his slender resources half a guinea a lesson, so anxious was he to improve himself, even in his manner of lecturing.
cards.locator: Chapter II. Life at the Royal Institution ¶19
cards.apply_it: Name the skill that matters most in your work. Find one person who could watch you do it and give you honest notes, and ask them this month.

quiz.question: What did Faraday do to improve his lecturing despite his small salary?
options: Paid for lessons from an elocutionist and invited critics to his lectures
Read his lectures word for word
Stopped lecturing until he was older
quiz.explanation: He paid half a guinea a lesson to B. H. Smart and later had Smart and Magrath criticise his delivery.

cards.title: Let your notes become questions, not just copied quotes
cards.body:
Faraday's early notebooks were full of extracts copied from books. As he grew as a scientist, his notes changed character. They became fewer quotations and more questions and problems to solve, such as whether pith balls diverge because of induction, or what happens if you distil a certain compound.

This shift marks the move from absorbing knowledge to producing it. Copying is a start, but a question gives your mind something to work on and tells you what to try next. When you study, try ending each session by writing the questions it raised rather than another summary.
cards.quote: His other notes now begin to partake less of the character of quotations and excerpts, and more of the nature of queries or problems for solution.
cards.locator: Chapter II. Life at the Royal Institution ¶20
cards.apply_it: At the end of your next study session, write three questions the material raised for you instead of a summary.

quiz.question: How did Faraday's notes change as he matured?
options: He began writing only in Latin
They shifted from quotations to questions and problems to solve
quiz.explanation: His notes moved away from excerpts and became queries and problems for solution.

cards.title: Keep a list of open questions and cross them off when solved
cards.body:
In 1822 Faraday started a notebook he called 'Chemical Notes, Hints, Suggestions, and Objects of Pursuit'. Into it went his own ideas and questions, including the line 'Convert magnetism into electricity', which nine years later became his greatest discovery.

Whenever a question found its answer, he drew his pen through it and added the date. At the front he wrote that he owed much to these notes and that anyone would find them worth the trouble after a year. An open list of the questions you want answered keeps big aims in view, and the dated crossings-out show you how far you have come.
cards.quote: I already owe much to these notes, and think such a collection worth the making by every scientific man. I am sure none would think the trouble lost after a year’s experience.
cards.locator: M. Faraday ¶20
cards.apply_it: Start a page titled 'Objects of Pursuit' and list five questions you want answered. Cross each one out with the date when you answer it.

quiz.question: What did Faraday do when a question in his notebook was answered?
options: Drew his pen through it and added the date
Copied it into a new book
Sent it to the Royal Society
quiz.explanation: He struck through each answered query and dated it, so the book recorded his progress.

cards.title: Be willing to admit you were wrong about love
cards.body:
As a young man Faraday filled his notebook with mocking rhymes against falling in love. Then he fell for Sarah Barnard, the daughter of a silversmith in his church. Her brother had told her about those rhymes, and she asked to see them.

Instead of defending his old views, Faraday sent her a poem confessing that he had written them out of ignorance and pride, and that he now repented. He asked her to turn from judge to friend and guide him to amend. Cynicism about love is easy to hold until you meet the right person. Admitting your change of heart honestly, even with some humour, is a good start.
cards.quote: But my fault I repent, and my errors detest; And I hoped to have shown my conversion in time.
cards.locator: H. Davy ¶8
cards.apply_it: Is there an opinion about relationships you have held mainly out of pride? Consider saying out loud, to someone you trust, that you have changed your mind.

quiz.question: How did Faraday respond when Sarah asked to see his rhymes against love?
options: He sent her a poem repenting of them
He asked her brother to explain
quiz.explanation: He sent a poem admitting he had written them out of ignorance and pride, and that he now repented.

cards.title: Declare your love without pressuring the other person
cards.body:
In 1820 Faraday wrote to Sarah Barnard to say he loved her. He was open about his feelings, yet he insisted he did not want to bend her affections for his own sake. He would serve her happiness by being present or by staying away, whichever was best, and asked only that she not withdraw her friendship.

Sarah was young and hesitated, unsure she could return feelings so strong. She went away to Ramsgate, and Faraday followed to spend time with her, and they came to an understanding. Honest feeling, offered with real respect for the other person's freedom, gives love room to grow rather than forcing it.
cards.quote: Let me, however, claim not to be the selfish being that wishes to bend your affections for his own sake only. In whatever way I can best minister to your happiness either by assiduity or by absence, it shall be done.
cards.locator: H. Davy ¶16
cards.apply_it: If you are courting someone, tell them clearly how you feel and also that their happiness and freedom to choose matter more to you than a quick answer.

quiz.question: What did Faraday promise Sarah in his letter declaring his love?
options: That he would never leave London
To give up science for her
To serve her happiness, whether by being near or by staying away
quiz.explanation: He said he would minister to her happiness either by assiduity or by absence, not bend her affections for his own sake.

cards.title: Keep the wedding simple and put the heart first
cards.body:
Faraday and Sarah Barnard married on 12 June 1821. His salary was only a hundred pounds a year, and they began married life in his rooms at the Royal Institution. Few guests were invited, because Faraday wanted the day to be 'just like any other day'.

He wrote that there would be no bustle, no noise and no hurry, since the pleasure they looked for was in the heart. Their marriage lasted forty-six years and became famous for its devotion. A wedding is one day; the marriage is the rest. Spending your energy on the relationship rather than the spectacle is a choice many couples still find freeing.
cards.quote: be no bustle, no noise, no hurry ... it is in the heart that we expect and look for pleasure.
cards.locator: H. Davy ¶22
cards.apply_it: If you are planning a big event with a partner, list together the three things that truly matter to you both and let the rest be simple.

quiz.question: What kind of wedding did Faraday want?
options: A ceremony at the Royal Institution theatre
A quiet day 'just like any other day'
quiz.explanation: He invited few people and wanted no bustle, noise or hurry, because the pleasure he sought was in the heart.

cards.title: Count your marriage above every honour you receive
cards.body:
Faraday received nearly a hundred honours from academies and universities across Europe, and kept their certificates mounted and indexed in a special book. In 1847 he slipped one extra entry into it: the date of his wedding.

He wrote that, as a source of honour and happiness, it far exceeded all the rest. Two years later he called his marriage the event that, more than any other, contributed to his earthly happiness and healthy state of mind. Achievements are easy to display and count. It takes a deliberate act to record that the person beside you matters more than any of them.
cards.quote: Amongst these records and events, I here insert the date of one which, as a source of honour and happiness, far exceeds the rest.
cards.locator: H. Davy ¶27
cards.apply_it: Write your partner, or someone you love, a short note saying plainly that they matter more to you than any achievement.

quiz.question: What did Faraday insert into his book of diplomas and honours?
quiz.explanation: He added his wedding date, saying it far exceeded all the other records as a source of honour and happiness.

cards.title: Celebrate breakthroughs with real, boyish joy
cards.body:
On 3 September 1821, working with his young brother-in-law George Barnard, Faraday saw a wire carrying a current revolve around a magnet for the first time. He danced around the table with a beaming face, crying out that they had succeeded at last. Then he proposed they finish the day at Astley's to see the horses, and off they went.

Faraday never lost this delight. Decades later he could still dance around an experiment or shout for joy at another man's success. Serious work and playful celebration are not opposites. Marking your wins, even small ones, keeps the creative fire burning through the long stretches between them.
cards.quote: There they go! there they go! we have succeeded at last.
cards.locator: M. Faraday ¶8
cards.apply_it: The next time something you have worked on finally works, stop and celebrate it properly with someone, before moving on to the next task.

quiz.question: How did Faraday celebrate his discovery of electromagnetic rotation?
options: He wrote to the Royal Society that night
He said nothing until it was published
He danced round the table and then went to see the horses at Astley's
He held a dinner for scientists
quiz.explanation: He danced around the table exclaiming 'There they go!' and then took George Barnard to Astley's.

cards.title: Stay grateful to those who helped you, even after they hurt you
cards.body:
Davy grew jealous of his former assistant's rising fame and actively opposed Faraday's election to the Royal Society. It was a painful betrayal, and their relationship was never quite the same afterwards. Yet Faraday allowed himself no resentment, and grew indignant if anyone raked up the old scandal.

Twenty years after Davy's death, the French chemist Dumas spoke coolly of him. Faraday said nothing, but took him to Davy's portrait and to the notebook where Davy had circled the words 'Capital Experiment'. Dumas was won over. Remembering what someone gave you, alongside how they let you down, keeps you generous and frees you from bitterness.
cards.quote: He was a great man, wasn’t he?
cards.locator: M. Faraday ¶30
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who helped you but later disappointed you. Write down one thing you still owe them, and let that be your main memory of them.

quiz.question: How did Faraday respond when a friend spoke coolly of Davy?
options: He showed him Davy's portrait and notebook and called him a great man
He agreed and listed Davy's faults
He refused to speak to the friend again
quiz.explanation: Despite Davy's opposition to his election, Faraday took Dumas to Davy's portrait and notebook and said, 'He was a great man, wasn't he?'

cards.title: Decide what you love more than money, and act on it
cards.body:
By 1830 Faraday was earning a thousand pounds a year from expert chemical work for businesses and the courts, on top of a salary of only a hundred. He could easily have made five thousand a year and died rich. Instead, finding the work ate the time he needed for research, he gave it up.

Within months he made his greatest discovery, magneto-electric induction, the principle behind every modern dynamo. Years later he turned down a publisher's open offer for his lectures, explaining that money was no temptation to him. Knowing what you value more than income makes hard choices clearer, though the right trade-off is different for everyone.
cards.quote: In fact, I have always loved science more than money; and because my occupation is almost entirely personal I cannot afford to get rich.
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Middle and Later Life ¶55
cards.apply_it: Write down one thing you would protect even if it cost you income. Then check whether your calendar this month reflects it.

quiz.question: Why did Faraday give up his well-paid expert work around 1830?
options: It was taking time he wanted for original research
quiz.explanation: He chose research over a fortune, and soon after made his great discovery of magneto-electric induction.

cards.title: Test last night's ideas first thing in the morning
cards.body:
His friend De la Rive described Faraday's working rhythm. Every morning he went into his laboratory the way a businessman goes to the office, and put the ideas he had had overnight to the test.

Just as important was his attitude. He was as ready to drop an idea if the experiment said no as to follow it through rigorously if the experiment said yes. Ideas are cheap and plentiful; testing them is what turns them into knowledge. A steady routine of trying things out, with no attachment to any one result, works for business plans and personal habits as well as for physics.
cards.quote: Every morning Faraday went into his laboratory as the man of business goes to his office, and then tried by experiment the truth of the ideas which he had conceived overnight
cards.locator: M. Faraday ¶54
cards.apply_it: Write down one idea tonight. Tomorrow morning, before anything else, do one small thing that tests whether it holds up.

quiz.question: What was Faraday's attitude when an experiment said 'no' to his idea?
options: He repeated it until it said yes
He was as ready to give the idea up as to follow it if the answer was yes
quiz.explanation: De la Rive said he was equally ready to abandon an idea or pursue it, depending on what experiment showed.

cards.title: A failure may mean the method is wrong, not the goal
cards.body:
Faraday was convinced that if electricity could make magnetism, magnetism should be able to make electricity. He tried in 1824 and twice in 1825, and recorded 'No result'. He tried again in 1828, and failed a fourth time. Others gave up or announced results they later withdrew.

Faraday read his failures differently. They didn't prove the search hopeless; they showed he hadn't yet found the right way to experiment. In 1831, on his fifth attempt, he found the missing piece: the magnet had to move. When something keeps not working, ask whether the goal is wrong or only the approach.
cards.quote: A third failure did not convince him that the search was hopeless: it showed him that he had not yet found the right method of experimenting.
cards.locator: Chapter IV. Scientific Researches: Second Period ¶4
cards.apply_it: Pick a goal you have failed at more than once. List three different methods you haven't tried yet.

quiz.question: What finally made Faraday's experiments to get electricity from magnetism succeed?
options: Moving the magnet relative to the coil
quiz.explanation: Earlier attempts failed because magnet and coil were at rest; on the fifth attempt in 1831 he found relative motion was needed.

cards.title: Carry a physical reminder of the problem you're solving
cards.body:
During the years he puzzled over how to get electricity from magnetism, Faraday carried a tiny model in his waistcoat pocket: an iron core about an inch long, wrapped in a few turns of copper wire. In spare moments he would take it out and look at it, using it to concentrate his thoughts on the problem.

A physical object keeps a question alive in the back of your mind, so small idle moments become thinking time. A sketch on your desk, a sticky note on your mirror or a prototype in your bag can do the same. Your mind keeps working on what it keeps seeing.
cards.quote: which model he at spare moments would take out and contemplate, using it thus objectively to concentrate his thoughts upon the problem to be solved.
cards.locator: Chapter IV. Scientific Researches: Second Period ¶4
cards.apply_it: Make a small physical reminder of a problem you want to crack, such as a sketch or card, and keep it where you'll see it in spare moments.

quiz.question: What did Faraday carry in his pocket while working on electromagnetic induction?
options: A tiny model of an iron core wrapped in copper wire
quiz.explanation: He carried a small coil-and-core model and looked at it in spare moments to focus his thoughts on the problem.

cards.title: When something works one way, ask if it works in reverse
cards.body:
In the 1820s scientists knew that an electric current could make a piece of iron into a magnet. Faraday had a habit of mind that never let a relationship rest at one direction. If electricity could produce magnetism, he asked, why shouldn't magnetism produce electricity? He wrote the challenge in his notebook in 1822: 'Convert magnetism into electricity.'

The answer, found in 1831, gave the world the dynamo and the electric power industry. Turning a known fact around is one of the simplest creative moves there is. If customers come to you, can you go to them? If a habit causes stress, could a reversed habit relieve it?
cards.quote: If it were possible to use electricity to produce magnetism, why should not the converse be true?
cards.locator: Chapter IV. Scientific Researches: Second Period ¶3
cards.apply_it: Take one thing you know works in your field and write down its reverse. Spend five minutes asking whether the reverse could also be true or useful.

quiz.question: What question led Faraday to his greatest discovery?
options: Can light be bent by gravity?
What is the smallest particle of matter?
If electricity can make magnetism, can magnetism make electricity?
quiz.explanation: He looked for the converse of electromagnetism and found that a moving magnet produces electric currents.

cards.title: Pause to get better tools, then let ripe ideas run
cards.body:
In September 1845 Faraday glimpsed a tiny effect of magnetism on light. It was so faint a newcomer would have missed it. Rather than straining at it, he wrote 'Have got enough for to-day' and stopped for several days while he borrowed a far more powerful magnet from Woolwich.

When it arrived, he filled twelve pages of his notebook in a single day and closed with the words 'An excellent day's work.' The pause had done double duty: better equipment, and time for his thinking to mature. Knowing when to stop and regroup is part of creative work, not a break from it.
cards.quote: His thoughts had ripened during the five days, and he advanced rapidly from point to point.
cards.locator: Chapter V. Scientific Researches: Third Period ¶30
cards.apply_it: If you are stuck on a project, ask what better tool, information or help you need. Stop, get it, and return with fresh eyes.

quiz.question: What did Faraday do after first seeing the faint magneto-optical effect?
options: Paused to obtain a more powerful magnet, then worked rapidly
quiz.explanation: He stopped for several days to borrow the Woolwich magnet; his ideas ripened and he then made rapid progress.

cards.title: Work, finish, publish: an unshared result barely counts
cards.body:
Early in his career Faraday suffered painful disputes over who had discovered what, and he learned that work left unfinished or unpublished invites confusion. In later life he was scrupulous about dating and promptly publishing his research.

His advice to the young chemist William Crookes was three words: work, finish, publish. He followed it himself, writing up major discoveries within weeks. It is a sound rule well beyond science. Ideas in drafts help no one and earn no credit. Doing the work is only the first step; seeing it through to completion and putting it in front of others is what gives it value.
cards.quote: To younger men he inculcated the necessity of proper and prompt publication of their researches if they would reap the benefit of their work.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. Views on the Pursuit of Science and on Education ¶13
cards.apply_it: Pick one piece of work that is nearly done. Set a date this week to finish it and share it with the people it is for.

quiz.question: What three-word advice did Faraday give to the young William Crookes?
quiz.explanation: He urged young researchers to publish properly and promptly, summed up as 'Work, Finish, Publish.'

cards.title: Do one thing at a time, finish it, and do a little if not much
cards.body:
Among the notes Faraday wrote to himself on cards were three short reminders. He told himself to tackle one thing at a time, to see each thing through to the end, and on days when he could not do much, to do at least a little.

Together they form a compact philosophy of steady work. Single-tasking guards attention. Finishing stops a pile of half-done projects from building up. And doing a little on difficult days, rather than nothing, keeps momentum alive. Faraday struggled with memory problems and periods of exhaustion, so these were practical rules for him, not slogans. They suit anyone juggling too much.
cards.quote: Remember to do one thing at once.
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Middle and Later Life ¶83
cards.apply_it: Tomorrow, choose one task, finish it before starting another, and on a low-energy day commit to just ten minutes rather than skipping it.

quiz.question: Which of these was NOT one of Faraday's reminders to himself?
options: Do a little if you cannot do much
Always work late into the night
quiz.explanation: His cards said to do one thing at once, to finish a thing, and to do a little if he could not do much.

cards.title: Try hard to succeed, but don't expect to
cards.body:
Another of Faraday's private notes reads: 'Endeavour to succeed, expect not to succeed.' Next to it he wrote: 'Aim at high things, but not presumptuously.'

It is a useful balance. Full effort gives you the best chance. Low expectations protect you from crushing disappointment when, as in most research and most lives, things don't work first time. Faraday failed four times before his greatest discovery, and many of his later experiments found nothing. He kept going partly because a negative result didn't shatter him. Aim high, work hard, and hold the outcome lightly.
cards.quote: Endeavour to succeed--expect not to succeed.
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Middle and Later Life ¶89
cards.apply_it: Before your next big attempt, write down what full effort looks like, and remind yourself that a miss will be information, not a verdict.

quiz.question: What did Faraday advise himself about success?
options: Expect success and you will get it
Endeavour to succeed, but expect not to succeed
quiz.explanation: He paired full effort with modest expectations, and also noted to aim at high things, but not presumptuously.

cards.title: Attack your own idea before others can
cards.body:
One of Faraday's reminders on a card was to criticise his own view in every way by experiment, leaving, if possible, no objection for anyone else to raise.

This is the opposite of defending an idea you love. Instead you become its toughest critic, hunting for weak points while there is still time to fix them. His friend De la Rive saw the same habit daily in the lab. Today you can apply it to a business plan, an essay or an argument with a friend: list the strongest objections yourself, and test them honestly, before you present it.
cards.quote: one’s own view in every way by experiment--if possible, leave no objection to be put by others.
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Middle and Later Life ¶90
cards.apply_it: Before sharing your next proposal or opinion, write down the three strongest objections to it and check each one.

quiz.question: What did Faraday aim to do with his own views?
options: Criticise them by experiment so no objection was left for others
quiz.explanation: He tried to criticise his own view in every way by experiment, leaving no objection for others to raise.

cards.title: Match your confidence to the strength of the evidence
cards.body:
Faraday was fearless in speculation. He framed countless hypotheses and readily threw out deep-rooted ideas when experiments pointed elsewhere. But he held every theory with some doubt.

In a lecture on matter he said the wisest thinker proportions judgement and confidence to the evidence, takes a fact as a fact and a supposition as a supposition, and stays aware of prejudice even when he cannot escape it. That discipline lets you be bold and accurate at once. Before you argue a point, ask yourself which parts you know and which parts you are guessing, and speak with confidence to match.
cards.quote: who holds his theory with some doubt--who is able to proportion his judgment and confidence to the value of the evidence set before him, taking a fact for a fact and a supposition for a supposition
cards.locator: The Four Degrees ¶4
cards.apply_it: Take one strong opinion you hold. Sort your reasons into facts and suppositions, and adjust how certain you sound.

quiz.question: According to Faraday, who is the wisest philosopher?
options: One who holds his theory with some doubt and proportions confidence to evidence
One who never changes his mind
quiz.explanation: He said the wisest holds theories with some doubt, taking a fact for a fact and a supposition for a supposition.

cards.title: Speak slowly enough for ideas to land
cards.body:
At twenty-one, Faraday wrote that a speaker's words should never be rapid and hurried, which makes them unintelligible, but slow and deliberate, so ideas pass easily into the listeners' minds.

He practised what he preached. In his early lectures he kept a card in front of him with the word 'Slow' written on it. If he forgot and sped up, his assistant Anderson was told to place the card before him. Nerves push almost everyone to rush. A simple, visible reminder is an easy fix, whether it is a sticky note on your laptop or a word at the top of your notes.
cards.quote: The utterance should not be rapid and hurried, and consequently unintelligible, but slow and deliberate, conveying ideas with ease from the lecturer, and infusing them with clearness and readiness into the minds of the audience.
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Middle and Later Life ¶29
cards.apply_it: Before your next presentation or important call, write 'Slow' where you will see it while you speak.

quiz.question: What word did Faraday keep on a card in front of him when lecturing?
quiz.explanation: He kept a card reading 'Slow', and his assistant would place it before him if he started to speak too fast.

cards.title: Spark interest at the start and keep talks under an hour
cards.body:
Faraday believed a speaker should catch the audience's interest at the very beginning and then, by gradual steps they barely notice, keep it alive as long as the subject needs. A flame should be lit at the start and kept burning brightly to the end.

For the same reason he disliked breaks in a lecture and long lectures. One hour, he wrote, is long enough for anyone. Both points hold for today's meetings and presentations. Open with something that makes people care, build steadily, and finish before attention runs out rather than after.
cards.quote: A flame should be lighted at the commencement, and kept alive with unremitting splendour to the end.
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Middle and Later Life ¶33
cards.apply_it: Rewrite the first minute of your next talk or meeting so it gives people a reason to care, and cut it to fit well within an hour.

quiz.question: What did Faraday think was the right maximum length for a lecture?
options: As long as the subject needs, however long
quiz.explanation: To keep the audience from tiring, he wrote that one hour is long enough for anyone.

cards.title: Don't apologise for small slips; it only draws attention
cards.body:
In his letters on lecturing, Faraday criticised speakers who angle for applause, run down their own abilities, fuss about how delicate an experiment is, or beg for indulgence nobody asked for.

He noticed something sharper too. Often most of the audience only became aware of an error because of the apology that followed it. His rule was to apologise as seldom as possible, and mainly when the problem actually affected the audience. When a slide is wrong or you stumble over a word, carry on. If it truly matters to your listeners, fix it briefly and move on.
cards.quote: I have several times seen the attention of by far the greater part of the audience called to an error by the apology that followed it.
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Middle and Later Life ¶34
cards.apply_it: In your next presentation, notice the urge to apologise for a small slip and simply continue instead.

quiz.question: What did Faraday notice about speakers' apologies?
options: They often draw attention to errors nobody had noticed
quiz.explanation: He saw that most of the audience often noticed an error only because of the apology that followed it.

cards.title: When you lose a word, pause instead of filling the gap
cards.body:
Among Faraday's rules for speaking, kept in his manuscript notes, were: never repeat a phrase, never go back to amend, and if at a loss for a word, don't stammer 'ch-ch-ch' or 'eh-eh-eh', but stop and wait for it.

He found the word soon comes, the bad habit breaks, and fluency follows. A short silence sounds far more assured to listeners than a string of ums. Another rule on the same list was never to doubt a correction someone else gave him, which is how he kept improving. Try letting a pause do the work the next time you search for a word.
cards.quote: If at a loss for a word, not to ch-ch-ch or eh-eh-eh, but to stop and wait for it. It soon comes, and the bad habits are broken and fluency soon acquired.
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Middle and Later Life ¶42
cards.apply_it: Record yourself explaining something for two minutes. Count your filler words, then try again using silent pauses instead.

quiz.question: What did Faraday advise doing when you can't find a word?
options: Go back and restart the sentence
Stop and wait for the word
quiz.explanation: He told himself to stop and wait for the word rather than making filler sounds; it soon comes and fluency follows.

cards.title: Show, don't just tell, even when it seems obvious
cards.body:
Faraday never merely told his audience about an experiment; he showed it, however simple and well known. He once told a young lecturer that if he said a stone would fall when he opened his hand, he would open his hand and let it fall.

He also opened each subject on its most familiar side and led listeners gently towards the unfamiliar, so they were taking in new facts before they noticed the transition. He even made quick models out of wood, wire, paper or potatoes. Whatever you explain, find something people can see as well as hear.
cards.quote: Take nothing for granted as known; inform the eye at the same time as you address the ear.
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Middle and Later Life ¶47
cards.apply_it: For your next explanation, add one thing people can see, such as a sketch, a demo or a real object, even for the simple parts.

quiz.question: What did Faraday say he would do if he told an audience a stone would fall?
options: Open his hand and let it fall
Ask the audience to imagine it
quiz.explanation: He took nothing for granted and would actually drop the stone, informing the eye as well as the ear.

cards.title: Explain to children clearly and share their sense of wonder
cards.body:
Faraday started the Royal Institution's Christmas lectures for young people and gave them nineteen times, the last on the Chemistry of a Candle in 1860. With adults his thoughts sometimes outran his hearers, but with children he was careful to be perfectly clear and never let his ideas run ahead of them.

Children loved his laugh and frankness. One listener said he looked at things with a boy's fresh wonder, like an inspired child. He said he had never found a child too young to understand what he told them; their questions afterwards proved it. Good explaining to the young means respect for their minds plus delight in the subject.
cards.quote: When, however, he lectured to children he was careful to be perfectly distinct, and never allowed his ideas to outrun their intelligence.
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Middle and Later Life ¶59
cards.apply_it: Explain something you love to a child this week. Keep each step clear, show them something real, and let your own enjoyment show.

quiz.question: What did Faraday say about children and science?
options: They should wait until secondary school
He had never found a child too young to understand what he told them
quiz.explanation: He told a Royal Commission he had never found a child too young to understand him, as their later questions showed.

cards.title: Real learning takes effort; easy lectures are not enough
cards.body:
Asked about popular evening lectures, Faraday was frank. Lectures that really teach will never be popular, he said, and lectures that are popular will never really teach. People who think science is easier to learn than the alphabet know little about it, and nobody learned the alphabet without pain and trouble.

He still valued lectures for showing an attentive listener what he really had to learn. That is a useful way to see videos and podcasts today. They can map a subject and spark interest, but the learning itself happens when you practise, struggle and test yourself.
cards.quote: They know little of the matter who think science is more easily to be taught or learned than A B C; and yet who ever learned his A B C without pain and trouble?
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Middle and Later Life ¶78
cards.apply_it: After your next lecture, video or podcast, close it and spend ten minutes recalling and practising what it covered without looking.

quiz.question: What did Faraday think lectures were good for?
options: Showing an attentive listener what he really has to learn
quiz.explanation: He held that lectures inform the mind and show what one has to learn, but real learning takes pain and trouble.

cards.title: Ask experts to put their conclusions in plain words
cards.body:
Faraday knew almost no mathematics beyond simple arithmetic and algebra, yet he worked closely with mathematical physicists. In 1857 he wrote to James Clerk Maxwell asking whether a mathematician's conclusions could be expressed in common language as fully and clearly as in formulae.

Maxwell, he noted, had always managed to give him a perfectly clear idea of his results, enough to think and work from. Faraday suggested experts should routinely offer their findings in this 'popular useful working state' as well as their own technical form. When you are the expert, translate. When you are not, ask without embarrassment.
cards.quote: When a mathematician engaged in investigating physical actions and results has arrived at his own conclusions, may they not be expressed in common language as fully, clearly, and definitely as in mathematical formulæ?
cards.locator: M. Faraday ¶28
cards.apply_it: Take one technical thing you know well and write a three-sentence version a non-expert colleague could act on.

quiz.question: What did Faraday ask Clerk Maxwell?
options: Whether mathematical conclusions could be expressed in common language
quiz.explanation: He asked whether mathematicians' results could be stated in common language, clearly enough for others to work from.

cards.title: Chase the knowledge, not the renown
cards.body:
People sometimes complained that Faraday never trained a successor. In a private note he puzzled over what makes someone succeed in science, and suspected many fail because they look to the fame and reward rather than to knowledge itself and the quiet delight of gaining it.

He had seen promising people whose eye was always on the world's praise. Such minds, he thought, carry a shade of envy or regret that makes discovery almost impossible. He added that he had looked long for a genius and never found one, but had seen many who would have succeeded with sound self-discipline. Motivation rooted in the work itself is steadier than motivation rooted in applause.
cards.quote: Do not many fail because they look rather to the renown to be acquired than to the pure acquisition of knowledge, and the delight which the contented mind has in acquiring it for its own sake?
cards.locator: The Four Degrees ¶9
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself honestly why you are pursuing your current goal. Write one reason that would still hold if nobody ever praised you for it.

quiz.question: Why did Faraday think many able people failed in science?
options: They looked to renown and reward rather than knowledge for its own sake
quiz.explanation: He believed seeking the world's praise brought envy and regret that blocked discovery, while self-discipline mattered more than genius.

cards.title: Turn down status that would pull you from what matters
cards.body:
In 1857 a deputation from the Royal Society urged Faraday to become its President, the highest place British science could offer. He had already declined a knighthood. After hesitating, he refused this too.

He told Tyndall privately that he must remain plain Michael Faraday to the end, and that if he accepted he could not answer for the soundness of his mind for a single year. Years earlier he had also declined a government pension when the Prime Minister called such pensions humbug; it was granted only once the matter was put right. Knowing your limits and your values lets you say no to honours that would cost more than they give.
cards.quote: I must remain plain Michael Faraday to the last; and let me now tell you, that if I accepted the honour which the Royal Society desires to confer upon me, I could not answer for the integrity of my intellect for a single year.
cards.locator: The Four Degrees ¶44
cards.apply_it: Consider a role or title you are being drawn towards. Ask what it would cost your health, focus or values, and decide with that in view.

quiz.question: Why did Faraday decline the Presidency of the Royal Society?
options: He wished to remain plain Michael Faraday and feared the strain on his mind
quiz.explanation: He told Tyndall he must remain plain Michael Faraday and could not answer for his intellect if he accepted.

cards.title: Say plainly when you have reached your limit
cards.body:
At the end of 1839 Faraday suffered a serious breakdown, with giddiness and failing memory. His doctor wrote that rest of body and mind was absolutely necessary. Faraday tried to keep lecturing, broke down again, and then rested for nearly four years, apart from a few lectures.

The illness distressed him. On scraps of paper he wrote notes to make his state clear: when he said he could not bear much talking, he meant exactly that, with no hidden meaning. He was being honest about a real limit. If you are exhausted, saying so directly, without apology or code, helps others help you, and seeking proper medical care is part of strength.
cards.quote: when I say I am not able to bear much talking, it means really, and without any mistake, or equivocation, or oblique meaning, or implication, or subterfuge, or omission, that I am not able
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Middle and Later Life ¶8
cards.apply_it: If you are running on empty, tell one person plainly what you can't manage right now, and consider speaking to a doctor.

quiz.question: What happened when Faraday tried to keep working after his doctor advised rest?
options: He suffered a more serious breakdown and rested for nearly four years
quiz.explanation: He kept lecturing in 1840, broke down more seriously, and then rested for nearly four years apart from a few lectures.

cards.title: Simple pleasures can help an overworked mind recover
cards.body:
During his long rest, Faraday filled his days with light things. He played games of skill, did paperwork crafts, and went to the theatre. He was one of the earliest members of the Zoological Society, and his wife recalled that the animals at the Gardens were a great resource to him when he was overwrought.

His niece said he loved acrobats and tumblers, and even a Punch and Judy show delighted him. In Switzerland he watched waterfalls, shepherds and cowherds. None of this was grand. When your mind is overworked, gentle, absorbing pleasures that ask nothing of you can be part of recovery, alongside proper medical care.
cards.quote: the Gardens were a great resource to him when overwrought and distressed in the head.
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Middle and Later Life ¶10
cards.apply_it: List three simple things that absorb you without effort, like animals, music or a walk. Book one of them into this week.

quiz.question: According to Mrs Faraday, what was a great resource to Faraday when he was overwrought?
quiz.explanation: She wrote that the animals at the Zoological Gardens were a continual interest and a great resource when he was distressed.

cards.title: Let your partner be your place of rest, and say so
cards.body:
In old age Faraday's memory failed badly. Writing to Sarah from Glasgow in 1863, he said his head and heart were full but his recollection was failing, even of friends in the same room. He longed to be home with her.

He asked her to take up again her 'old function' of being a pillow to his mind and a rest. Years before he had written that outings into the world only made him value the quiet pleasures of home more. Friends saw how tenderly he led her to her seat when she was lame. Telling your partner what they are to you, especially when life gets harder, is part of keeping love strong.
cards.quote: You will have to resume your old function of being a pillow to my mind, and a rest, a happy-making wife.
cards.locator: The Four Degrees ¶53
cards.apply_it: Tell your partner, or someone close, one specific way they give you rest or steadiness. Use your own words, out loud or in a note.

quiz.question: How did Faraday describe his wife's role in his 1863 letter?
options: A pillow to his mind and a rest
quiz.explanation: With his memory failing, he wrote that she would resume her old function of being a pillow to his mind and a rest.

cards.title: Faraday kept his faith and his science in separate rooms
cards.body:
Faraday was a lifelong, devout member of the small Sandemanian church, and served as an elder and preacher. Yet he did not try to prove his faith with science or use science to argue for it.

To Lady Lovelace he wrote that he saw no need to tie the study of nature and religion together. He believed nature could never contradict the things of faith, but in daily life the religious and the philosophical were two distinct things for him. His biographer thought few minds could divide themselves so strictly, and readers may differ on that. Still, his example shows a person of deep faith and rigorous science living with integrity in both.
cards.quote: in my intercourse with my fellow creatures, that which is religious and that which is philosophical have ever been two distinct things.
cards.locator: Chapter VIII. Religious Views ¶10
cards.apply_it: Reflect: where do faith or deeply held values and evidence each speak in your life, and how do you keep both honest?

quiz.question: How did Faraday see the relationship between his religion and his science?
options: He used experiments to prove God
He kept them as two distinct things
quiz.explanation: He wrote that the religious and the philosophical had always been two distinct things in his dealings with others.

cards.title: Some commitments are between you and God alone
cards.body:
A month after his wedding, Faraday made a public confession of sin and profession of faith before his church, which his wife already belonged to. He did it without telling her beforehand.

When Sarah asked why, he answered that it was between him and his God. His friend Tyndall said that in fifteen years Faraday never raised religion unless asked, and then spoke simply, without trying to convert. For Faraday, faith was too sacred to parade. Even in the closest marriage, there can be a personal space of conviction that belongs to one person, honoured rather than resented.
cards.quote: It was an act of humility the more striking in that it was done without any consultation with his wife, to whom he was so closely attached, and who was already a member of the congregation.
cards.locator: Chapter VIII. Religious Views ¶8
cards.apply_it: Reflect on one conviction that is truly your own. How do you hold it with sincerity without needing others' approval?

quiz.question: What did Faraday say when his wife asked why he hadn't told her about his profession of faith?
options: That is between me and my God
quiz.explanation: He replied that it was between him and his God.

cards.title: Hold your faith firmly and others' faiths with respect
cards.body:
Faraday's church was small and strict, yet his own faith was gentle towards others. Tyndall said it was held in perfect tolerance of other people's beliefs, and that it strengthened and beautified his life.

When Cardinal Wiseman asked whether he believed the whole true Church was contained in his little sect, Faraday said, 'Oh, no!' but that he believed from the bottom of his soul that Christ was with them. Deep conviction and humility about others need not conflict. You can be sure of what sustains you while leaving room for others to find their own way.
cards.quote: this faith, held in perfect tolerance of the faiths of others, strengthened and beautified his life.
cards.locator: Chapter VIII. Religious Views ¶6
cards.apply_it: Have a conversation this week with someone whose beliefs differ from yours, aiming only to understand what sustains them.

quiz.question: How did Faraday answer when asked if the whole Church was shut up in his small sect?
options: Oh, no, but he believed Christ was with them
Yes, only his sect was true
He said religion did not matter
quiz.explanation: He said 'Oh, no!' while affirming from the bottom of his soul that Christ was with his own congregation.

cards.title: Choose the poor neighbour's tea over the grand dinner
cards.body:
Faraday was famous and constantly invited by the great and noble. Members of his chapel said he would decline when he could, preferring to visit a poor member in trouble, help her from his own purse, drink a cup of tea with her, read the Bible and pray.

He gave away a large share of his income quietly, so quietly that no record survives of how much, and he visited the sick. For Faraday faith showed itself in kindness to people who could give him nothing back. It is a quiet test anyone can apply: where does your free time and money actually go?
cards.quote: but he would, if possible, decline, preferring to visit some poor sister in trouble, assist her, take a cup of tea with her, read the Bible and pray.
cards.locator: Chapter VIII. Religious Views ¶24
cards.apply_it: This week, give an hour to someone who is lonely or struggling and can offer you nothing in return, even just a visit over tea.

quiz.question: What did Faraday prefer to dining with the high and noble?
options: Visiting poor members of his church in trouble
quiz.explanation: He preferred to visit a poor sister in trouble, help her, take tea with her, read the Bible and pray.
